newsitem.title: FRANCE: Moslem fundamentalists on trial after Paris blast.
newsitem.headline: Moslem fundamentalists on trial after Paris blast.

text.p: The trial of 34 Moslem fundamentalistsfor backing Moroccan guerrillas opened in Paris on Monday, with defendents saying they were indoctrinated by their religious leaders at holiday-like breaks in the French countryside.

Tight security blanketed the trial as it opened. Police said they feared new attacks after a Paris rush-hour train bombing in which four people died last week. Investigators say plans to try the militants may have motivated the bombers.

The cases have not been formally linked but anonymous telephone threats have been received warning of fresh attacks unless France releases detained Moslem fundamentalists. Only 21 of the 34 accused were in the dock as the trial began.

Six others, including three French passport-holders, are held in Morocco -- three of them awaiting execution and three sentenced to life terms there. Another, Algerian Djamel Lounici, was detained in Italy. The rest are sought by authorities.

The 34 are accused of criminal conspiracy in connection with a terrorist enterprise. They are alleged to have backed guerrilla violence in Morocco in 1994, including the robbery of a Marrakesh hotel in which two Spanish tourists were shot dead and a gunfight with police in Fez.

One of the defendents, Farid Zaouali, 25, said he was taught about weapons and explosives at a camp in Afghanistan. On his return to France, he followed others "courses" in Orleans, or in the mountains of central France. "For us, it was a holiday-camp," he said.
El-Moustapha Ben Haddou, 24, said he had been fascinated by the personality of presumed leader Mohamed "Said" Zinedine, 36. "We went out on picnics and marches (in the mountains)," he said.

Both Ben Haddou and Zaouali said they had been chosen to attack nudists on a Tangiers beach in Morocco in August 1994. Prosecutors say they failed to find any nudists, considered attacking police but gave up on the idea and returned to France.

The 34 were among nearly 200 Moslem fundamentalists detained after a wave of bomb attacks in France in 1995 in which eight people were killed and 160 injured. Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA) claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying France supported the military-backed Algerian government.

Nearly all of the accused are French Moslems in their mid and late 20s, children of Algerian or Moroccan immigrants recruited in run-down, high-rise suburbs near Paris, Orleans and the eastern town of Besancon which have large Arab minorities.
Prosecutors say they were recruited by Morocco's outlawed Islamic Youth Movement whose aim was to overthrow King Hassan and create an Islamic government.
The group also had support from Algerian fundamentalists. Lounici is accused of membership of the armed wing of the Algerian Islamic Salvation front (FIS).
The prosecution says the accused were sent for weapons training aboard, including to Afghanistan, and that they carried out hold-ups in France as well as Morocco to finance their activities.
But most of their missions were either botched or not carried out at all, according to the prosecutors.

Officials said 20 people were still in hospital after last Tuesday's train bombing. Another 92 had been treated for wounds or shock. Investigators say they suspect the bomb was set off by Algerian Moslem rebels because of similarities to the 1995 wave of attacks.
